title: The pillar of fire with no end
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hookLine: Brahma and Vishnu race to find the end of a pillar of fire, and Shiva's great night keeps watch beside it
carry: shivaratri: a night awake for the god without end

lines: A PILLAR OF FIRE, NO END.
cards: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing about which of them is greatest, when a pillar of fire splits the dark between them. It has no top they can see, and no bottom. So they agree: whoever finds an end wins.
Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go for ages.
Neither finds anything. And then Shiva steps out of the fire.

teach.h: THE PILLAR IS SHIVA, WITHOUT END.
teach.b: In the Shiva Purana's telling, the pillar of light is Shiva himself, without beginning or end, and the stone linga in every Shiva temple remembers it.
Many Hindus tell this as the story of tonight's festival, and in many South Indian temples the middle of the night of Shivaratri is kept as the hour the pillar appeared. The name says it plainly.
It falls in the dark half of the lunar month, the night before the new moon, when there's almost no moon to see by. The Shiva Purana describes the vow for it. Fast through the day.
Worship Shiva in the linga, with water and bilva leaves.
Stay awake until morning. Notice what kind of teaching this is. Nobody hands you a lecture.

teach.h: THE NIGHT TEACHES THROUGH THE BODY.
teach.b: The night teaches through the body: hunger, sleepiness and the dark each take away something you usually lean on, and ask what's left. Brahma and Vishnu tried to measure Shiva and couldn't.
On Shivaratri, people stop measuring and simply stay awake beside him. Some keep every hour in a crowded temple until sunrise. Some keep part of the night at home.
The days ahead take it in order: the vow, the fast, keeping awake, the name, the offerings, and dawn.

how: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus who keep it may fast, visit Shiva temples or worship at home, offer water, milk and bilva leaves to the linga, and stay awake through the night with chanting and singing.

games.q: a friend asks why Hindus worship Shiva as a linga, a simple stone shape. what's the story behind it?
o: it's a statue nobody ever finished carving.
a pillar of fire with no end appeared, and Brahma and Vishnu couldn't find its edges.
it marks the place where Shiva was born.
games.why: in the Shiva Purana's telling, the linga remembers the pillar of light with no beginning and no end. on Shivaratri people stop measuring and stay awake beside it.

practice: Dim the light around you if you can, or simply close your eyes, and notice what the dark takes away, the screen, the faces, and what it gives back: sounds you hadn't heard, the weight of your body, the breath.

Keep your attention on one thing, and come back to it whenever you drift. If you pray, let that one thing be Shiva's name, om namah shivaya, or the name of God you use; if you don't, the breath is enough.

wordCard.voice: Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. Today, its story: the pillar of fire with no end. And its shape: a fast, worship, and staying awake until dawn.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Shivaratri, the night of Shiva.
